analysis.one_liner: Requires federal agents policing protests to identify themselves and limits federal crowd control to federal property.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2025 with 11 Senate supporters and sent to the Judiciary Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require any federal law enforcement officer, military member, or contractor policing a protest or riot to display their agency and name or a unique identifier at all times, and it would bar them from covering that information up or using unmarked vehicles to make arrests. It would restrict federal crowd control to federal property and its immediate surroundings unless a state's governor and a local government jointly ask for help in writing, or the Insurrection Act is invoked. It would also require agencies to publish, within 24 hours of deploying personnel, how many agents were sent, where, what the mission is, and where any detained civilians are being held.
analysis.who_benefits: Protesters, demonstrators, and residents of communities where federal agents are deployed. The bill gives people stopped or arrested by federal agents a way to know who is arresting them, and it creates a public record of federal deployments and detention sites.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Protesters and communities near federal deployments

how_it_helps.text: Federal officers and military members policing demonstrations, riots, or civil disobedience must visibly display their agency and last name or unique identifier, and cannot tape over or obscure it.

Federal officers and military members may not use unmarked vehicles to apprehend, detain, or arrest civilians during protest-related enforcement, and arrests made in violation of the identification or location rules are unlawful.

Federal crowd control is limited to federal property and the immediately adjacent sidewalk and street, unless a state governor and a local government head jointly request assistance in writing or the Insurrection Act is invoked.

Within 24 hours of any crowd-control deployment, the responsible agency must post on its public website the date, the number of personnel in each locality, the mission, the location and custody of any detained civilians, and any written assistance request.

analysis.who_pays: Federal law enforcement agencies, military units used for domestic enforcement, and any contractors performing law enforcement functions. They would lose the ability to operate anonymously or unilaterally outside federal property, and would face new public-reporting duties. Arrests made outside the rules would become unlawful, exposing improper actions to legal challenge.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal law enforcement agencies and contractors

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves significant exceptions: the restrictions do not apply once the Insurrection Act is invoked, and federal assistance can proceed whenever a governor and a local government head jointly request it in writing, so the limits depend heavily on those triggers.
The bill covers only federal officers, service members, and their contractors; state and local police at demonstrations are unaffected and remain governed by their own rules.

Supporters of agent anonymity have generally argued that publicly identifying individual officers can expose them and their families to harassment, a real cost an honest supporter of identification requirements must weigh against the accountability benefit; that trade-off is the core disagreement in this debate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits go to accountability for a specific power: agents who police protests without visible identity cannot be held to answer by anyone afterward, and unmarked-vehicle arrests have repeatedly caused public alarm. The costs fall on federal agencies' operational flexibility and, per the standard objection, on officer personal safety from public identification. The identification and notice rules are the strongest parts; the Insurrection Act exception means the bill's limits evaporate precisely in the situations of greatest concern, which a critic would call the bill's central weakness.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on July 22, 2025, joined by Sens. Wyden, Van Hollen, Hirono, Duckworth, Murray, and Warren as original cosponsors.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which is the only action it has received.
It has 10 Democratic cosponsors and 1 Independent cosponsor, with no Republican support in the Senate.

The bill would require visible identification for federal agents policing protests, ban unmarked vehicles for protest-related arrests, confine federal crowd control to federal property except on a joint state-and-local written request or an Insurrection Act invocation, and require public notice of deployments within 24 hours.
The bill makes arrests unlawful when conducted in violation of the identification or location restrictions.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal law enforcement agencies and the executive branch are better off: without floor action, the current rules — including anonymous policing of protests and unilateral federal deployments — remain in place unchanged.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 22, 2025 and has taken no action since; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not brought the bill to the floor; with no committee action and no Republican cosponsor, there is no path to a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: Every supporter is a Democrat or Independent (10 Democrats and 1 Independent cosponsored); no Republican has signed on, and the bill has not advanced in the Republican-controlled Senate.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement agencies (including immigration and homeland security agencies used for protest enforcement)
industries.note: The bill strips these agencies of the ability to police protests anonymously, use unmarked vehicles, or deploy outside federal property without a state-and-local request, and makes noncompliant arrests unlawful. Their interest in operating without visible accountability runs directly against the public's interest in knowing who is arresting them.

The bill's definition explicitly covers contractor and subcontractor personnel performing law enforcement functions, so contractors policing protests would face the same identification, unmarked-vehicle, and location limits as federal officers.

industries.industry: Incumbent officeholders and the executive branch generally
industries.note: The bill is a check on executive-branch power over domestic policing and creates a public record of deployments and detentions, reducing the branch's discretion to act unilaterally.

analysis.trajectory: The realistic path is that the bill stays in the Judiciary Committee until the Congress ends. It has no Republican support, the committee is chaired by the majority party, and no markup or hearing has been scheduled; bills of this type almost never reach the floor without either a chairman's decision or a floor-leader exception.
